t: Definition & Objective: NOTA (None of the Above) is an electoral option provided on ballot papers and Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) enabling voters to exercise a negative vote and formally reject all contesting candidates in secret.
Judicial Origin: Directed by the Supreme Court of India in the landmark judgment PUCL v. Union of India on 27 September 2013.
Constitutional Foundation: The Supreme Court linked the right to register a negative vote in secrecy with the Freedom of Speech and Expression under Article 19(1)(a).
1982: First experimental use of Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) in the Parur Assembly constituency, Kerala.
1993: Introduction of Electors Photo Identity Card (EPIC / Voter ID).
4 September 2013: VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) introduced and first used experimentally in the Noksen Assembly by-election, Nagaland.
27 September 2013: Supreme Court directs mandatory introduction of the NOTA button on EVMs.

t: Automatic Invalidation Fallacy: Statement claiming "If NOTA receives the majority/highest votes, the election is cancelled and a fresh poll is held" - FALSE; Legal Position: Under the First-Past-the-Post system, even if NOTA receives the maximum votes, the contesting candidate securing the highest number of valid votes among the candidates is declared elected.
Abstention vs. Active Participation: Exercising NOTA is NOT non-voting/abstaining; it is the active exercise of the statutory right to vote by registering a neutral/negative choice.
Rajya Sabha Elections: NOTA is NOT applicable in Rajya Sabha and Legislative Council elections (struck down by SC in 2018; limited to direct Lok Sabha & Assembly elections).
Nature of Doctrines: Most constitutional doctrines in India are judicially evolved concepts—they are NOT expressly defined or written in the text of the Constitution.

c: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Parliament's constituent power to amend the Constitution is plenary but limited; it cannot abrogate, alter, or destroy its essential foundation/basic features.
Marbury v. Madison (1803) (Chief Justice John Marshall, USA)
Power of the higher judiciary (SC + HCs) to adjudicate on the constitutional validity of legislative acts and executive actions.
A.K. Gopalan (1950) / State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)
Only the offending/unconstitutional portion of a statute is declared void, leaving the valid rest intact if they can be separated.
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P. (1955)
Pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are not dead ab initio, but remain overshadowed/dormant (eclipsed) and become active if the FR is amended.
Prafulla Kumar v. Bank of Commerce (1947) / State of Rajasthan v. G. Chawla (1959)
Resolves legislative field overlaps; examines the true nature and essence of a law rather than its incidental encroachment on another List.
Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar (1952)
"What cannot be done directly, cannot be done indirectly"—transgression of legislative competence masked under a permissible guise.

t: Shankari Prasad (1951) & Sajjan Singh (1965): Upheld the 1st CAA; ruled that ordinary law under Art. 13(2) does not include constitutional amendments under Art. 368 (Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights).

under: Constitutional Amendment Battle (Art. 368 vs Part III)
t: Golaknath (1967): Overruled earlier cases; held that an amendment is "law" under Art. 13(2) and Parliament cannot abridge or take away any Fundamental Right.

under: Constitutional Amendment Battle (Art. 368 vs Part III)
t: Kesavananda Bharati (24 April 1973): Delivered by the largest bench (13 Judges; 7:6 majority); held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution (including FRs), but cannot damage or destroy the "Basic Structure".

under: Constitutional Amendment Battle (Art. 368 vs Part III)
t: Minerva Mills (1980): Reaffirmed that a limited amending power is itself a Basic Feature; invalidated clauses (4) and (5) of Art. 368 inserted by the 42nd CAA.
Textual Fallacy: Statement claiming "The term 'Basic Structure' is explicitly defined in Part XX of the Constitution" - FALSE (Judicially formulated concept).

Fundamental Rights Absolute Immunity Trap: Statement claiming "Fundamental Rights can never be amended post-Kesavananda" - FALSE; Correct Principle: FRs can be amended, provided the amendment does not violate the Basic Structure.

Judicial Review as Basic Structure: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980), and L. Chandra Kumar (1997), Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 was explicitly declared an inviolable part of the Basic Structure.

India vs UK Constitutional Model: India: Constitutional Supremacy + Judicial Review of primary legislation; United Kingdom: Parliamentary Sovereignty (No striking down of primary parliamentary statutes).

Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part XI (Articles 245–255) and the Seventh Schedule, operationalized through Article 246 (Subject distribution) and Article 246A (Special provision for GST via 101st CAA, 2016).
Three-Fold Distribution (Article 246): List I (Union List): Parliament has exclusive legislative competence (Art. 246(1)).
Three-Fold Distribution (Article 246): List II (State List): State Legislatures have exclusive legislative competence (Art. 246(3)).
Three-Fold Distribution (Article 246): List III (Concurrent List): Both Parliament and State Legislatures have concurrent legislative competence (Art. 246(2)).
Residuary Powers (Article 248): Legislative competence over any subject NOT enumerated in any of the three Lists is vested exclusively in Parliament (e.g., Space Research, Cyber Law).

Repugnancy Rule (Article 254): In case of conflict between Central and State legislation on a Concurrent List subject, the Central law prevails (Unless the State law was reserved for Presidential assent and received it under Art. 254(2)).

t: Residuary Power Locus: Under Article 248, residuary legislative powers lie exclusively with Parliament (In the USA and Australia, residuary powers lie with the States; in Canada and India, they lie with the Centre).

GST Dual Competence (Art. 246A): Article 246A gives simultaneous powers to both Parliament and State Legislatures to frame laws regarding Goods and Services Tax (breaking the strict exclusive-list dichotomy of Article 246).
Local Self-Government Placement: Panchayati Raj and Municipalities are strictly enumerated in List II (State List, Entry 5).
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part V, Chapter IV (Articles 124–147).

Inauguration & Predecessor: Inaugurated on 28 January 1950; succeeded both the Federal Court of India (established under the Government of India Act, 1935) and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
Strength & Parliament's Power: The power to increase the number of Supreme Court judges is vested exclusively in Parliament by law (Art. 124(1)).

Retirement Age & Removal: Judges retire at 65 years of age (Art. 124(2)); removed by the President following an Address supported by a Special Majority in each House of Parliament on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity (Art. 124(4)).

t: Article 141 (Binding Precedent): The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within the territory of India.

Article 142 (Complete Justice): Empowers the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order necessary for doing "Complete Justice" in any cause or matter pending before it; Operates unhindered by ordinary statutory limitations.

Curative Petition (Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra, 2002): Evolved by the Supreme Court under its inherent powers anchored in Article 142 to prevent abuse of process and cure gross miscarriages of justice after a review petition under Article 137 has been dismissed.

SLP Armed Forces Exception (Art. 136(2)): Special Leave Petitions do NOT lie against judgments/sentences passed by courts-martial or military tribunals.
Advisory Opinion Binding Status (Art. 143): Opinions rendered by the Supreme Court to the President under Article 143 are strictly advisory and NOT binding on the President.
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part VI, Chapter V (Articles 214–231); Article 214 mandates a High Court for each State.

Historical Origins (Indian High Courts Act, 1861): 1866: High Court for North-Western Provinces established at Agra (shifted to Allahabad in 1869).
Strength Determination (Art. 216): The strength/number of judges for each High Court is decided and fixed by the President of India (NOT Parliament, NOT the Governor/Chief Minister).

Article 215: High Courts to be Courts of Record (Evidentiary value + Power to punish for contempt).
Article 216: Composition of High Courts (Chief Justice + judges appointed by President).
Article 217: Appointment and conditions of the office of a Judge of a High Court.
Article 218: Application of certain provisions relating to Supreme Court (Removal) to High Courts.
Article 220: Restriction on practice after being a permanent Judge.
Article 221: Salaries, allowances, and pensions of Judges.
Article 222: Transfer of a Judge from one High Court to another by the President.
Article 223: Appointment of Acting Chief Justice.
Article 224 / 224A: Appointment of Additional/Acting Judges & attendance of retired Judges.
Article 226: Power of High Courts to issue certain Writs.
Article 227: Power of Superintendence over all courts and tribunals by the High Court.
Article 230: Extension of jurisdiction of High Courts to Union Territories.
Article 231: Establishment of a Common High Court for two or more States/UTs.
Appointment Consultation Matrix (Art. 217): Chief Justice of HC: Appointed by President after consultation with the CJI + Governor of the State.
Appointment Consultation Matrix (Art. 217): Other HC Judges: Appointed by President after consultation with the CJI + Governor + Chief Justice of that High Court.
Qualifications (Art. 217(2)): Citizen of India AND; Held a judicial office in India for ≥ 10 years OR; Practiced as an advocate of a High Court for ≥ 10 years
Qualifications (Art. 217(2)): Trap: Unlike the Supreme Court (Art. 124(3)(c)), there is NO provision for appointing a "distinguished jurist" as a High Court judge.

Removal Mechanism (Art. 217(1)(b) r/w Art. 124(4)): Removed ONLY by the President following an Address passed by each House of Parliament by a Special Majority on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

Post-Retirement Practice (Art. 220): A retired permanent HC Judge CANNOT plead/act before any court or authority in India, EXCEPT the Supreme Court and other High Courts (where they did not serve as a permanent judge).
Writ Scope (Art. 226 > Art. 32): High Court writ jurisdiction is broader in scope than the Supreme Court because it extends to Fundamental Rights + Any other legal purpose/right.
Writ Scope (Art. 226 > Art. 32): High Court writ power is discretionary; Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right.
Supervisory Jurisdiction (Art. 227): High Court exercises administrative and judicial superintendence over all subordinate courts and tribunals throughout its territorial jurisdiction.
Supervisory Jurisdiction (Art. 227): Armed Forces Exception: Does NOT extend to courts and tribunals constituted under any law relating to the Armed Forces (Art. 227(4)).
Parliament has the power under Article 231 to establish a Common High Court for two or more States and UTs.

Oath vs Resignation Head Trap: Oath administered by the Governor of the State (Art. 219); Resignation submitted to the President of India (Art. 217(1)(a)).
Salary vs Pension Source Trap: Salaries & Allowances: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State; Pensions: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

t: Acting Chief Justice (Art. 223): Appointed by the President from among HC Judges when the office of Chief Justice is vacant, temporarily absent, or unable to perform duties.
Additional Judges (Art. 224(1)): Appointed by the President due to temporary increase in court business or arrears of work for a period not exceeding 2 years (Cannot serve beyond 62 years of age).
Acting Judges (Art. 224(2)): Appointed by the President when a permanent Judge is temporarily absent or acting as Chief Justice (Ceases at 62 years).
Retired Judges at High Court Sittings (Art. 224A): The Chief Justice of a High Court (with President's prior consent) may request a retired HC/SC Judge to sit and act as a High Court Judge.

under: High Court Chief Justice: Judicial vs. Administrative Capacity
t: When acting in an administrative capacity (e.g., staff appointments, disciplinary actions), the Chief Justice of a High Court is subject to the writ jurisdiction (Art. 226) of another Judge of that same High Court.

under: High Court Chief Justice: Judicial vs. Administrative Capacity
t: The Chief Justice enjoys no absolute immunity from judicial review regarding administrative decisions.
The Dual-Fund Trap for High Court Judges: Salary & Allowances: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Art. 202(3)); Pensions: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 112(3)(d)(iii)).

Post-Retirement Practice Trap: Supreme Court Judge Cannot practice in ANY court/authority in India; High Court Judge Can practice in the Supreme Court and other High Courts (where they were not a permanent judge).
Oath vs. Resignation Head Trap: High Court Judge's Oath Administered by Governor; High Court Judge's Resignation Addressed to President.
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part XIV-A (Articles 323-A & 323-B); inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
Core Nature: Quasi-judicial, specialized dispute resolution bodies created to reduce pendency in regular courts and provide domain expertise.

Judicial Review Anchor (L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997): The Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review of the High Courts under Article 226/227 and the Supreme Court under Article 32 is an integral part of the Basic Structure.
Judicial Review Anchor (L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997): Clauses excluding the jurisdiction of High Courts and the Supreme Court in Articles 323-A and 323-B were declared unconstitutional.

Judicial Review Anchor (L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997): Decisions of tribunals (like CAT) are subject to scrutiny before a Division Bench of the concerned High Court before approaching the Supreme Court.

c: Exclusively covers public service matters (recruitment & conditions of service of Union, State, local/statutory authority employees)

t: Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT): Established in 1985 under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 (Article 323-A).
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT): Has original jurisdiction over service matters of civil servants under the Union.
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT): Appeals against CAT orders lie before the Division Bench of the jurisdictional High Court (L. Chandra Kumar rule).
Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT): Established under the TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2000 (Original parent act: TRAI Act, 1997).
Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT): Adjudicates disputes in telecom, broadcasting, and airport tariff matters.

Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT): Appellate Routes: Telecom/broadcasting/tariff appeals lie directly to the Supreme Court on substantial questions of law; cyber appellate orders route to the High Court.
National Green Tribunal (NGT): Statutory body established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 (Guided by principles of Natural Justice, not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908).
National Green Tribunal (NGT): Appeals against NGT orders lie directly to the Supreme Court (within 90 days).

Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act [IMDT Act, 1983]: Struck down as unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005) on the grounds that it violated Article 355 (Duty of the Union to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance).

t: Part Number Misattribution: Any option placing Tribunals in Part XI (Relations between Union and States) or Part X (Scheduled & Tribal Areas) is FALSE - It is strictly Part XIV-A.

Enactment Power Distinction (Art. 323-A vs 323-B): State Legislatures have NO power to enact laws under Article 323-A (Vested exclusively in Parliament); State Legislatures CAN enact tribunal laws under Article 323-B on subjects within their legislative competence.

Armed Forces Exception: High Court's superintendence under Article 227 does NOT extend to courts and tribunals constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces (Art. 227(4) / Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007).
